intro: Twelve verses, one of the eight psalms of David in the closing group that runs from 138 to 145, and the plainest lament in that group. The shape is easy to hold: two verses of request, four of description, six that are almost nothing but imperatives. Two words carry it. The speaker's own spirit appears twice and fails both times, in verses 4 and 7, and then in verse 10 he asks for a different spirit, God's. And the word servant opens the argument in verse 2 and closes it in verse 12, so everything asked for in between rests on that and on nothing else.

stichs.en: A psalm of David.
LORD, hear my prayer, give ear to my pleas;
in Your faithfulness answer me, in Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The opening is doubled twice over: two verbs for hearing, two nouns for what is being said, two divine attributes to answer by. Faithfulness and righteousness are named before any trouble is.

stichs.en: And do not come into judgment with Your servant,
for no living thing is righteous before You.

verses.summary: The request is qualified immediately, and the qualification is the strangest thing in the psalm: answer me, but not by judging. The reason given is universal rather than personal, which takes the speaker's own case out of the argument.

stichs.en: For an enemy has pursued my soul,
crushed my life to the ground,
made me sit in dark places like those long dead.

verses.summary: The trouble in three clauses of increasing weight: pursued, crushed, made to sit. The third is the worst because it is not violence but an address, among people dead so long that nobody remembers them.

stichs.en: And my spirit grew faint upon me;
within me my heart is appalled.

verses.summary: The damage turns inward. Both verbs are things the speaker undergoes rather than does, and both locate the injury inside his own body rather than in his circumstances.

stichs.en: I remembered days long ago,
I have pondered all Your work,
I muse on the doing of Your hands.

verses.summary: The only move the speaker makes on his own. Three verbs of memory and thought, all aimed backwards at what God has already done, which is the usual way out of this in the psalms.

stichs.en: I have spread out my hands to You;
my soul is like a weary land for You. Selah.

verses.summary: Hands out, soul dry. The comparison is to land and not to a thirsty person, so what is described is not appetite but ground that can produce nothing at all until it rains.

stichs.en: Answer me quickly, LORD, my spirit has failed;
do not hide Your face from me,
or I shall be like those going down to a pit.

verses.summary: The imperatives begin, and the first one is about speed. The pit here is not a threat from the enemy but the ordinary end of anyone God stops looking at.

stichs.en: Make me hear Your kindness in the morning, for I have trusted in You;
make me know the way I should walk,
for to You I have lifted my soul.

verses.summary: The first request for something other than rescue. Morning answers the dark places of verse 3 and a way to walk answers the ground he was crushed onto, and both are asked on the basis of trust rather than merit.

stichs.en: Rescue me from my enemies, LORD;
with You I have covered myself.

verses.summary: The shortest verse in the psalm, and its last word is a genuine problem. Whatever the verb turns out to mean, the direction is the same: not away from the enemies but toward God.

stichs.en: Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God;
let Your good spirit lead me on level ground.

verses.summary: The centre of what the psalm actually wants. Not deliverance but instruction, and the spirit doing the leading is God's rather than his own, which has already failed twice.

stichs.en: For the sake of Your name, LORD, give me life;
in Your righteousness bring my soul out of distress.

verses.summary: Back to the two attributes of verse 1, and again the reason lies outside the speaker. Your name, not my case, is what the request is standing on.

stichs.en: And in Your kindness cut off my enemies,
and destroy all the foes of my soul,
for I am Your servant.

verses.summary: The one harsh verse, and it sits in the same breath as the word kindness, which is uncomfortable and deliberate. The last three words are the whole argument compressed: I am Your servant.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 1 and 2 ask to be heard and then rule out one way of being answered. Verses 3 to 6 describe the situation, moving from what an enemy did, to what happened inside the speaker, to one image of dry ground. Verses 7 to 12 are a run of ten or so imperatives and jussives with no narrative between them. The word soul appears five times, at {{3.3}}, {{6.3}}, {{8.13}}, {{11.7}} and {{12.6}}, and it is the object of nearly everything that happens: pursued, thirsty, lifted, brought out, harassed. The two attributes named at {{1.8}} and {{1.10}} return at {{11.4}} and, as kindness, at {{8.2}} and {{12.0}}. Nothing in the psalm reports that any of it worked.

{{9.4}} is the crux. The verb is from the root for covering, and the clause reads to You I have covered, with no object at all. It has been read as I have hidden myself with You, taking the speaker as the object; as I have covered my soul, supplying the noun from the neighbouring verses; and there is a long standing proposal that the original consonants held a different verb meaning to flee, which some ancient versions appear to reflect. The Masoretic text supports the first two, and it is the Masoretic text this page prints. A second point, at {{2.3}}: the plain object marker is doing the work of the preposition with, so the verse is about entering judgment alongside someone rather than about judging them. Third, {{10.10}} is a level plain, from the same root as the words for upright and straight, so being led on level ground is at once a request for easy walking and for a straight life. Fourth, the two thinking verbs of verse 5 are not silent ones: {{5.3}} is the verb behind the noun higayon and denotes a low murmur, and {{5.8}} is a rare verb closer to talking something over aloud than to reflection.

Verse 2 is the verse this psalm is remembered for. It does not claim the speaker is innocent and it does not concede that he is guilty. It says the category itself does not survive contact with God, and it says so about every living thing rather than about him, which is why the verse is quoted far outside its own psalm. One traditional line joins it to Ecclesiastes 7:20, that there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins, and treats the pair as the reason prayer asks for kindness instead of for a verdict. A second line works on what the psalm does with the word righteousness. At verse 2 righteousness is the thing nobody has; at verses 1 and 11 God's righteousness is the thing that rescues. The same root that would convict in a court is what the speaker appeals to for release, and that reversal is the real argument of the psalm. In Christian tradition this is the last of the seven penitential psalms, a grouping formed in late antiquity that has no Jewish counterpart.

Read the three occurrences of the word spirit in order and the psalm has a plot its surface does not show. At {{4.2}} the speaker's own spirit wraps itself over him, a verb used elsewhere of a garment and of fainting, so the breath that animates him becomes a covering that smothers him. At {{7.4}} the same word is finished, worn out, using the verb that Psalm 84 uses for a soul spent with longing. Then at {{10.6}} he stops asking anything of his own spirit and asks for God's, and the adjective attached to it, good, is the only positive word in the last six verses. On the mystical reading the whole psalm is that exchange: what a person carries runs out, and what is asked for at the end is not more of the same but a different source. The dry land of {{6.4}} works the same way. Land cannot water itself, and the image is chosen precisely because it removes the speaker's own agency from the picture.
